utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Ms. April Carter and Ms. Carmela Javier for the Prosecution, and I'm Dan Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Tina Drolec, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Carter will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Dr. Helge Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, what is your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My area of expertise is my demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Demography is the science that studies population change and population composition and the components that affect population size and composition, and the most important components are births, deaths, and migrations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, wouldn't you like the witness to place his name on record?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, will you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My name is Helge, first name, H-E-L-G-E, Brunborg, last name, B-R-U-N-B-O-R-G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You were describing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could call the speak all the speakers kindly be asked to pause between questions and answers to allow for the interpretation to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm certain that you heard that --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: -- we've been prohibited from speaking over each other. Probably the best way to handle this is -- for both English speakers is that if you will wait until the transcripts stop flowing before you answer the question. Sir, what education and training have you received to develop your expertise?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I have a masters degree from the University of Oslo and a PhD from the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What are those degrees in?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Both are in economics but with a strong -- large part being demography, especially at the University of Michigan. That is why I went to the University of Michigan, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, how does that training and education relate to the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I studied economics and demographic methods, demographic history, and all the aspects of demography that you need to know about, especially methods, are important.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What type of methods did you study?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mathematical methods, making projections, making estimates, statistical methods, but later I also learned through my work special methods.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And what of those trainings and special methods have you learned now?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm now -- I've worked mostly at Statistics Norway, and we rely a lot on administrative records or data from different administrative sources where one important issue to link data from different sources to make an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How long have you been employed in this profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: More than 30 years. 30, 35 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in this 30 or 35 years, have you ever been called upon to study demographics with relation to war victims?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I was called -- I was asked to work here in 1997, and I applied for a job here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What role did you serve here at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was asked to -- well, I was first seconded and later hired for one and a half years, full time. I was asked to study the demographic consequences of the armed conflicts in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did you later have any sort of specific focus, or did you remain solely in the armed conflicts in Bosnia at large?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I started mid-1997, and in late 1998. I -- or early 1999, because I continued as a consultant, I was asked to study the number of missing and dead related to the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Have you been asked to produce reports in relation to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the question had been: "Did you later have any sort of specific focus, or did you remain solely in the armed conflicts in Bosnia." And I thought -- is Srebrenica not in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can clarify a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1997, what was your specific focus?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My focus was to study the demographic consequences of the conflicts in Bosnia because the Tribunal, the OTP, felt that there were so many numbers floating around on -- say on the number of deaths, that ranged from 20.000 to 328.000, and which number could be relied on, so they felt the need for somebody with some experience and expertise on population statistics and demography.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you're are referring to the statistics between 20.000 and 328,000, are you referring to Bosnia at large?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, your work predominantly has been focused on Srebrenica in the past few years. How did you stop working on Bosnia in large and specifically focus on Srebrenica specifically?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because the office of the Prosecutor gave priority to that, and most of this was work -- was actually done after I went back to Norway. So it was done as a consultant, and a lot of work was done of my research assistants here who were based here, and I communicated -- I commuted and we communicated by e-mail and by telephone. So that is why, then, I was attached to the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you said you had consultancy with persons here at the ICTY, who were those persons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The first one who worked was Henrik Urdal of Norway. He was once my student, and the second was Torkild Lyngstad, also Norway. He was also my student, at one stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once you began focusing on Srebrenica, were you asked to produce any reports?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to produce a report in early 2000 in the trial against Krstic. I produced two reports, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To date, how many reports have you produced before the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think seven or eight on Srebrenica and two on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to your methodology in producing these reports. When producing a report such as the ones that are -- have been admitted before the Tribunal, what is the first step that you must take?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course, the first is the problem what are -- what do we want to study? What is the subjects? And I was told it was mainly how many were killed in the fall of Srebrenica on 12 July 1995; and secondly, I had to look for data sources that could illuminate this; and the third was what kind of methods and how to scrutinize these data sources and to do the analysis and come up with the reliable figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Since you've already stated what the study was supposed to be related to, can we now move on to the sources that you used?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were for all of Bosnia the figures of a number of deaths varied tremendously, and the figures for Srebrenica also varied from, say, 10, 15.000. My approach very early already in 1997, to study the consequences in Bosnia, was to rely on data on individuals, because it is much more difficult to lie or to cheat about data on individuals. If you rely on numbers in newspapers and so, other reports, you cannot be sure what the source is, how they were collected, if they are not double counting and so on, but if you have the name and date of birth and the particulars of every victim, then you can be much more sure that you have good data.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What sources did you use in order to determine who these individuals might be?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: On Srebrenica, I was told that the -- the international committee for the Red Cross, the ICRC, had collected data on missing and dead in Srebrenica from the family members of those who went missing. That was the most -- that was the primary source for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were there any secondary sources that you used?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I also learned that an American organisation, Physicians for Human Rights, PHR, had done similar things, although -- collected data on missing persons, although for a different purpose. They wanted to use those data who identify people who were exhumed in graves, whereas the ICRC collected data to help locate family members, preferably surviving family member.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Since 1997, have you relied upon any other sources in order to produce reports?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. It's important to see who lived in Srebrenica and surrounding areas before 1995, so we got hold of a copy of the census in 1991 with data on every individual that was enumerated in 1991, 4.3 million for all of Bosnia. And it's also important to see who the survivors were, so we got hold of copies of voters lists for all of Bosnia for 1997 and 1998, collected by the OAC, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. Moreover, we gradually -- I went on many trips to Bosnia to collect data. We gradually learned about other mostly minor sources of varying quality, such as, if you allow me, a database collected by the Muslims against genocide, lists of dates and names on tombstones, hospital records, displaced persons, dead soldiers, lots of different records. Some of these were discarded as being of little interest, not adding anything, or being of poor quality or being irrelevant for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Once you identified all of the data sources upon which you were going to rely, what methodology did you implement in order to analyse these documents?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first we had the list of missing persons. Actually, we had two different versions from the ICRC, so we had to merge these and weed out duplicates. So one individual was only represented once. We also have the list from the PHR that I mentioned, so we merged that with the ICRC. We then had the list for all of Bosnia. Then we needed to define who was related to the -- for the events in Srebrenica in 1995, so we defined then that only deaths occurring after or people who went missing - reported missing, I should say - after 1st of July, 1995, until the end of 1995 should be included; and only people who were reported [Realtime transcript read in error, "deported"] as going missing in - was it approximately - eight municipalities in Srebrenica and surrounding Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is there a certain name for the methodology in which you used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise. I believe that there is on line 13 a typo, and I believe it should be "... only people who were reported as going missing...", not "deported."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see "reported" on line 13, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see "deported."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are looking at different screens then or in different courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The sentence begins with the word "... and only people who were..." and the word that I'm referring to in my screen is -- on line 13 is "... deported as going missing in..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, it appears that the LiveNote that we're receiving through e-court is different than the LiveNote that we're receiving through our own individual PCs. The one that Mr. Guy-Smith is looking at does in fact say "deported," so the main screen coming through that's being reported out into the audience does say "deported."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to deal with whatever line it is. It's either 13 or 14. The word that I'm concerned about is "deported." I believe that the witness said "reported," although I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You're looking at line 14 -- what you are talking about is at line 14. Okay. Fine. And only people who were deported as going missing, or reported as going missing, where it says "deported." Yes. May the correction be made, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take in hand that I should probably skip a line if I jump up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Depends which screen we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter. You were asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that -- or I was beginning to ask you, was there a name for the type of methodology that you used in order to analyse the missing in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is called record linkage, since we have data for -- from different sources covering samples that include -- often include the same individuals. We need to make sure that we do not include one individual twice. We can also match records from widely different sources, say, such as the census 1991 and the missing in 1995, widely collected -- widely different, large sample and a small sample, and the purpose of matching these - we call it matching - is to find out, for example, if the people who were reported missing in 1995 actually lived in Bosnia in 1991 and that they were real persons and they were not -- these were not made up for political or other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The first question I would like to ask with regards to record linking is, is this method used other places beyond the research that you've completed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I used it myself in other circumstances in Norway where it is widely used.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How is it used?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is much easier to use because we have unique identification number. There are errors sometimes in that number in a country like Norway, too, but it's mostly very -- of high quality. The Nordic countries, the Netherlands use this method extensively. United States use it based on social security number to, say, link data from different sources, tax data, income data, security data and so on. And it is also used to study conflicts, say, in Cambodia, Patrick Everline [phoen] has used a similar method. It has been used for many years in historical demography, developed by the French historical demographer Louis Henry, where you had, say, in the 17th century, you had data from parish records, from church books on baptisms, confirmations, marriages, deaths. And you see the same name, say, John Smith in 1740, you see being baptized; you see the same name in 1795, John Smith. Is it the same John Smith? So you have to collect, compare data, and then do this to reconstitute the families. That is the term. And it's based on record linkage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, specifically for your work here at the ICTY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Here at the ICTY, what specifically did you do in order to match those records?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We -- since in the former Yugoslavia there was a unique identification number called "matic nibroj," [phoen] but it was not recorded for everybody in the census. It was not recorded at all by the ICRC or PHR. It was recorded for many in the voters list, so we could not rely on that alone. We had to rely on name and date of birth, and if that was not enough, place of birth, place of residence and so forth, and father's name also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is this unique identification number work, sir? Can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia, it was based I think on the 81 census. And so a number is assigned to each person in the population in Yugoslavia and in Norway. Also, it consists of the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this a national identity number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In some countries, it includes information such as a date of birth and gender and sometimes region. I believe in United States, the social security number is just a serial number. It doesn't include any information at all, so they are different methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If a person did not possess this personal information number, how did you match and make certain that you didn't have any duplicates in the list of missing for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If we compared two lists, to databases and saw that the first name, family name, father's name, date of birth, place of birth were identical, absolutely identical, we concluded that this was the same person, and if, also, there was nobody else with the same particulars, unique, what you'd call a unique match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But where do you get all this data from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, in the 1991 census, the data was recorded. In the numeration, people were -- enumerators went around and as in the regular census, they asked for each household, the recorded names and date of birth and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how did you find out about those people who were born after the 1991 census but before the massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there is that margin of error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Fortunately, there were very few if any children under the age of 4, 4 and a half, that are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the census was take on the 31st of March, 1991, and the fall of Srebrenica was on 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then those children who are 3, or 3 and 4, were eventually not accounted for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, there were no children -- the youngest person that was reported as missing from Srebrenica was a girl, age 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: True, but that's relying on reports from people. You are not relying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is relying on -- yeah, on victim's families that reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. And if a victim's family didn't report, then you have no knowledge about that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, and, also, if a whole family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was killed, then you had no -- so these are most probably under counts of the number of missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still interested to find out from whom or from which institution you went to find the data about date of birth, baptism, unique identification number. The person is dead with his ID card, and the birth certificate, we don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. So for the ICRC list of missing persons, this information was reported by family members of the victims, most often wives and mothers and other relatives. But they often did not know or have these certificates. They did not know exactly, remember, when was, say, my father born. They remember the year most often, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But could they remember his unique identification number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. So it was not included in the ICRC list, but in the census, then people -- many people say -- I think 60 percent, had papers showing the identity number, and they could then report that to the enumerator who wrote it down. That is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are saying that in fact it's a 60-percent certainty, that there could be 40 percent unaccounted for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But then for these people, the 40 percent, we have other information such as first name, family name, father's name, date of birth, and place of birth, so we have a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I go back to my question. Where do you find that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got it from the Federal Statistical Institute in Sarajevo, because they computerized all the information as -- after the census was taken in March 1991. It was computerized and put on a big file that we got a copy of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For entire Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. A very valuable source of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've enumerated two batches of people, the first are those persons with the personal identification number, as well as a group of people who had full data such as the first name, last name, father's name, place of birth. Are these the only persons that you've included in your count of the missing from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, because sometime after the fall of Srebrenica, other organisations started collecting data, first the Physicians for Human Rights, the PHR. Exhumation started, I believe, in 1996 or 1997, first by ICTY, and when they exhumed people with certain clothing, teeth, and so on, they could relate that to the information collected from the victim's families and later through DNA analysis. So then more and more data appeared on exhumed bodies. That is these bodies were identified with name -- by name, and most of these names were found on our list of missing persons. But they were -- in addition -- there were some additional persons that were identified, a few hundred that were not reported as missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you had a number of sources which you've received data from. How did you ensure that you didn't have duplicates?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Through the same record linkage. For example, we compared the list of missing persons to the post-war lists of voters, because in principle, a person cannot be -- cannot both be missing and registered to vote. Then something is wrong. So we thought that if a person had been listed -- reported to vote, registered to vote, in principle that person could be a survivor and not be missing anymore, but for some reason he or she did not report that they were survivors. The other thing that could happen is that the -- somebody cheated when registering to vote, to -- for political reasons, other reasons, or there could be just an error or mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, is the methodology that you've just listed the methodology that you've used for all reports that you produced in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We have also -- if I may, also looked at other sources. Sometimes we do not mention the sources because we find that they're either of poor quality or it is covered already or irrelevant, such as Muslims Against Genocide. We have also looked at lists of displaced persons, dead soldiers names on tombstones with date of death, et cetera. So we have tried everything that we could to find out if there were survivors amongst the missing or if there were more missing or if there were -- some of them were dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 12 February 2000, did you produce a report entitled "Report on the Number of Dead and Missing in Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders this report, 65 ter number 1374, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 1374 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, on 2 May 2000, did you produce a report entitled "Srebrenica Missing, Persons Reported Missing After the Takeover of the Srebrenica Enclave By the Bosnian/Serb Army on 11 July 1995"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1375 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1375 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 12 April 2003, did you produce a report entitled "Addendum on the Number of Missing and Dead from Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1376 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1376 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P406.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 25 January 2004, did you produce a report entitled "2004 Addendum to the List of Missing Persons from Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1378 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1378 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P408, Your Honours. 407, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 25 August 2004, did you produce a report entitled "Rebuttal Report, Blagojevic et al, IT 02-60, Regarding the Report on the Number of Missing and Dead From Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1377 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 16 November 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. With regard to the last Exhibit which is P480.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. P408. My document indicates that it's strictly confidential and to remain sealed. Does that still remain the case?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak up, please, for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Interpreter? The interpreter says please speak up for their benefit. Bring your mic closer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to P408, my copy indicates that it is labelled at strictly confidential, to remain sealed. I wonder whether that is still the case or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, do you want it under seal, ma'am, or do you want it just as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document can go in as a public exhibit with the exception of I'd have to double-check to see if there are any ICMP reports or graphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's ICMP?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The International Commission for Missing Persons produces quite a bit of data, and that does have privilege attached to it. I don't believe this report has any attached to it because all records that I have seen is that it's allowed to be a public exhibit, but I do want to double-check that before making a definitive answer to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you rather, then, have it under seal until you've checked?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That sounds fine, Your Honour. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit P408 under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. P408 is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 16 November 2005, did you produce a report entitled "Missing and Dead from Srebrenica, the 2005 Report and List"?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1379 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And finally, on 21 November 2005, did you produce a report entitled "Identified Persons Among the Missing and the Dead From Srebrenica, an Addendum to the Expert Report, Missing and Dead From Srebrenica, the 2005 report and list"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 1381 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On 21 November 2005, how many persons were identified as being missing from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Approximately 4.000 missing. If you -- no, sorry. 2.694. Excuse me. 7661 were on the OTP list of missing from Srebrenica. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you've obviously given some lower numbers. What were the other figures that you were giving that were related more to the 2.000s?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry for the confusion. The lower number, 2.694 persons, were the number of persons that had been confirmed dead through DNA analysis done by -- through reports from the ICMP, the International Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How did these reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Now, these are confirmed dead as a result of what incident actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people -- there have been a number of exhumations of mass graves in the Srebrenica area related to the fall of Srebrenica, and when these -- a new mass grave is found, it's investigated, exhumed, the bodies or the remains of the bodies are collected, and tests are taken from the bones. There's DNA analysis, which is then compared with the DNA samples from the victim's family, close family members. And so if there's a close family member, then you can see if there's a match.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm going to object. That's outside of the area of this gentleman's expertise as to how DNA works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, the answer goes beyond my question. My question was simply, confirmed dead as a result of what incident? And all I wanted to know, when you say, as of 21st November, 2005, 2.694 people were confirmed dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the total number of people that were confirmed dead as a result of the Srebrenica incident of the 10th of July or 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was the total number confirmed dead at that point in time based on the report from ICMP received sometime before 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait just a second. Let's try to listen to each other and focus on the question. I want to know whether this number, 2.694, was the total number as at 21st of November, 2005, confirmed dead as a result of the incidents of the 10th and 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is my understanding of this also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the location from which the bodies that the DNA testing was performed on, where that location was?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Where the bodies were exhumed from?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen reports on this. I haven't seen any mass graves myself, but my understanding is that they were exhumed from sites related to the incidents in Srebrenica where -- sites close to executions, places, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object. That answer is none-responsive. "Are you aware of the location from which the bodies that DNA testing was performed on, where that location was?" And he has not given us a location. He is speculating. And I think with regard to the question that you asked earlier, Your Honour, specificity is of some critical moment at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, where were the bodies exhumed from?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: From mass graves in many different places. I remember some names. Kravica, there were several mass graves, but I do not remember all the names. These have been presented in previous cases to -- at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I'm going to object. What has been done in previous case is a different matter. Unless he has personal knowledge of that, he is not competent to testify with regard to what occurred in previous cases. If he can once again cite us to specific testimony and specific locations, I have no objection whatsoever, but the speculative nature of this testimony is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, where are your witness's reports? Why doesn't he look at his reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly. He actually has his reports in front of him, and I would invite him to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. I'm happy do that. I'm looking for a list of all the sites and -- let me see. I'm looking at -- let me see. Excuse me. I don't remember if there was a list of all the sites in the 2005 report or whether that was collected -- was given in other reports. Let's see. It refers to Dean Manning's testimony in Popovic on 10 to 12 December 2007, a report I've read, which lists all the mass graves with the number of exhumed bodies from each mass grave. I obviously don't know -- remember the names of all those sites, but there were a number of sites with, as I said, the number in each grave that has been exhumed and identified. I hope that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you give me a page and reference number, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. In -- let me see. Sorry. I was now referring to a report, another report, submitted by Ewa Tabeau and Arve Hetland on 11 January 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, for a bit more clarity, with regards to these persons that you identify as 2.594 [sic], how did those persons relate to your missing list of 7661?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They have been found. All those names have been found on our lists --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: -- are missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you developed that list, you had indicated to the Court previously that that list was developed partially based on the reports of family members and other persons that these people were missing from Srebrenica at or around this time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So the persons that have been identified through DNA testing, you are indicating that they are also persons who have been identified as missing around the time of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. How did these reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: May I ask one question in relation to the connection between forceful dislocation or migration and the concept of missing persons. When you report about missing persons, does that include only those who have been confirmed dead or includes also those who have perhaps forcefully migrated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does not include those -- it only includes those who are believed to be dead. At the beginning, very few of them were confirmed dead. But it does not include those who were forcibly removed if families knew about that. Only those -- so if a family was forcibly removed but other relatives knew that they were forcibly removed to somewhere else, they would not report them as missing. But the purpose of the ICRC list is to help in locating family members because in a chaotic war situation then often they lose contact. This was also before mobile telephones were common. It was not -- before internet. It was not easy to locate people when they had lost contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Second question. You have presented us with a methodology, and you say that statistics were very important. Is that a sort of inferential statistics considering the number that a given population existed at the time and then the number of that decreased population at another point in time? What I'm saying is that we are confronted here with many figures. One, those who have been exhumed and identified, 2.694, your own figure of missing persons of 7661, and these two figures are different in nature because one refers to a strictly confirmed death identified and exhumed, and the other, 7661, is a figure derived from investigations related to the census, other means of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 7661 is based on reports from family members, but only -- but we have checked to eliminate duplicates, and we have checked to see whether these are real persons, and we found most of them, not all, but we found I think about 83 percent on the 1991 census. So you are correct. These are of a different nature. But the smaller figure supports the bigger figure because we started out with 66 confirmed deaths in 2000. It has now grown to almost 3.000, and it is still growing. Reports come from the ICMP on new identified deaths all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Now, there is a perhaps a third type of figures, those who come from comparing two populations at a different point in time, and then you specify those that may have been caused by natural death according to the rate of death during a given time, you know, and then out of that, you see the deviation between the situation in the census versus to the real number in reality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. And initially, that was my -- the approach I was thinking about, comparing population -- pre- and post-war population size, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Have you applied any kind of a statistical measure like chi-squared in your first report to see the deviation between these two figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My studies on this is not based on the inferential statistics. It is not based on parabolistic distribution. It is based on purely on individual cases that we have added together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So at no moment in your studies you adduce inferential statistics to project decreases in population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Madam Carter, but I've got one or two questions to also clarify. Sir, the number 2.694, is it a part of or additional to 7.661?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is a part of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And as it increases, does the 7.661 also decrease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you confirm a person dead and he was missing, you've got to reduce on that side and increase this side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you do reconcile the two as you go along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in addition, every time new reports come to ICMP, if there are a few additional names that were not on our list of missing persons because they were not reported as missing, so it -- there's a small difference between, say, 100 and 200 that has been added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about reconciliation of the missing and the dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Of course, a person cannot be both missing and dead. You are absolutely correct. So then we strike off missing and change the status to dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please refrain from overlapping for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you had indicated that when you initially began this study, you had I think you said 66 persons confirmed dead, and now we are moving into mid-2000s. Can you explain to the Court to the extent that you know why these numbers are increasing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They are increasing because there are new exhumations, because there are -- there's ongoing work on DNA analyses, and the Defence is absolutely correct. This is not my area of expertise, but I've sort of tried to understand the basics of it. I cannot tell you any details on DNA analysis, but -- this is very difficult work, DNA analysis. But my understanding is also that in recent years, it has been automated. Previously, DNA analysis was done through manual visual comparison. Now there's a lot of computerization that goes on, so this work is much more efficient. There's several issues that complicate this. One is that there are bones found in many graves, the so-called tertiary -- secondary and, also, tertiary graves, and often the -- sorry, it's very time-consuming. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't want you to go into the area that the Defence is objecting to. I think you've answered Madam Carter's question to the extent that it had been put.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, based on this trending from 2000 through 2005, do you anticipate this number to stay the same, to decrease, or to increase?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I expect very strongly that the number of dead -- confirmed deaths will increase and the number of still missing will decline. As in 2005, approximately one-third, 31.5 percent to be exact, of the list of missing persons had been identified as dead. It will certainly increase.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You've also indicated that ICMP continually produces reports. Are you aware of any additional reports since 2005?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. There have been several, and we are in the process of analysing those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to consult with co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution passes the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before I ask you any questions, I want to make sure that I'm being heard, that I'm speaking loud enough. Could somebody in the interpretation -- if you could just tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Close enough to the microphone. That's the trick. Loud doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to start off by seeing if I can understand some relatively basic information. You obtained data from a census that was done in March of 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The data that you obtained from that particular census included, in no particular order, the names of individuals.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First name and last name.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The sex of the individual.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On occasion, the ethnicity of the individual?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The date of birth, if I haven't said that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I may add the father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, father's name. And on occasion, there was a unique identification number.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is that the sum total of the information that existed in that particular database? Are we missing anything?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. You are missing some educational attainments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Economic activity, religion, language, mother tongue. I don't remember if there's a question -- there's a question, I think, on number of children ever born to the women, because the purpose of a census is really to map the population with regard to a number of demographic and social factors. Names are not -- are reported to make sure that everybody is counted. It's not part of the statistical exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the 1991 census, the next time that you received what I'm going to call for the moment - and bear with me - purely objective information would have been when you were looking at the voter lists in 1997; is that correct? When I'm saying "purely objective information," I'm doing that from the standpoint of it's information that contains no particular, let's say, familial concerns with it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, you might say that. I also received minor data, databases, minor collections of varying quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the information that you received in 1997, the information concerning voter lists, could you tell us a little bit about what information was contained with regard to those voter lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There was first name, family name, in some for large number but for all cases the unique identification number, date of birth, sex, I think municipality of birth or municipality of residence at least. The municipality they were registering in to vote, the municipality they wanted to vote for. So there were four different municipality numbers recorded in the voter's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to those two databases alone, and we'll discuss the other databases that you used, but with regard to those two databases alone, then you would have a number of factors that should match with regard to individuals, let's say, who are for the moment not missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those would be first name, family name, date of birth, sex, and to the extent that you have a unique identification number, those would be kind of large factors upon which could you rely in order to make a determination of what extent of the population still remained from the 1991 census. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a fair statement, but they are not missing, of course. There are also natural deaths, emigration, and all kind of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And errors, don't forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right, right. With regard to the 1991 census, that particular census, could you tell us what the error rate was concerning the data that was compiled in terms of that census? Do you understand what I mean by error rate?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. You need to define the error rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. By error rate, I mean, to what extent is the census that you were given in 1991, that database, a completed accurate census of the number of people who were in the area in total?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is not known because to do that you need to have -- do a what is called a post-enumeration survey, which I don't think was done, or use some other method to really determine the number of people who were not enumerated. There -- always, some are missed. That is always the case. United States has going very far into estimating the error rate or the proportion, the coverage, and they have all kinds of post-enumeration service because then, say, the taxes depend on the population size and transfers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Without taxes, no infrastructure, and we know where that leads.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the post-enumeration numbers, could you explain to us very briefly, and then we're going to take a break, what occurs? How does that come about.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In the post-enumeration survey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Then a sample is reinterviewed. So there are new -- I think usually new enumerators go to the same households. They select a few areas, and they go to the same, and they ask the same questions again, and they ask -- and they compare to see how complete was the previous. There's another issue, and that is also whether it's the de jure or de facto population that is enumerated. Is it the people who are actually found in the house or in the place on the census day? Should it include people who are temporarily absent? Should it include workers who -- say, people who are temporarily in Germany working? Those are some -- where different countries have different principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate time to take a break, or am I early?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not yet. You are too early, 15 minutes early.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, great. I was a bit worried. I looked at the clock, and I was making a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've mentioned de jure and de facto population. With regard to the census that was taken in 1991, one of the factors that was in fact occurring at that time in 1991 was that there was a certain percentage of the population - and I don't know what that percentage was; I'm hoping you might be able to help us here - that was absent from Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I believe so, but I do not know the percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether or not that particular piece of information, the percentage that was absent in 1991 with regard to the census that was done, was accounted for in that census, and by that I mean, are the people who are recognised in the 1991 census, people who are in fact in situ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or are they those people that you've referred to who may be doing temporary work outside of the country or may have actually moved permanently outside of the country but have not yet been registered as having moved outside?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My impression from studying says -- this is in the former Yugoslavia in that year, is that it was primarily a de jure census, and there was a tendency to include people who are temporarily absent, sometimes for long periods, perhaps permanent. But if a person -- a man is asked, who are the members of your household, he would tend, then, to list all his sons, also those that lived abroad for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of that is a cultural issue with regard to the manner in which the people living in that particular region perceive family?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, independent of the issue of that percentage, which is an unknown percentage, as I think you've explained, were you able to make a determination with regard to the 1991 census as to whether or not there were any unique factors of identification with regard to - and now I'm going to use this in a generic sense - the area known as Srebrenica; or was the census that was done with regard to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina the same as with regard to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There was one census for all of Bosnia, and it was -- enumeration was done by -- for each municipality, is optional, and there was also -- each municipality was divided into smaller areas called "kru" [phoen] or something, I believe, so then they divided using maps, all of each municipality, including Srebrenica, into smaller areas. Then one or more enumerators had the responsibility to cover their areas and include -- enumerate everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And based upon your analysis of the 1991 census and the data that you received from that census, could you tell us what -- two things. One is, what are the towns or areas that comprise Srebrenica -- Srebrenica region as a whole; and two, what was the population of that area in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it's awhile since I worked on this. I got it in 1997, but I think -- well, of course, yeah, Potocari as one part, so there were several -- municipality of Srebrenica consisted of the town of Srebrenica, and smaller places, Potocari was one of them. And I do not recall the names of all others. I've been to Srebrenica and travelled around, but I do not recall them. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of the population of that particular area, can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it's 34, 35.000 in the municipality. The total population was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I recall in a previous time you testified there had been rumours of as many as 40.000.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is a different number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just a lawyer, but thank you very much for the...

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The 1991 census -- that was 1991 figure. I think when -- the 40.000 figure may have referred to the number of people believed to be in Srebrenica before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very good.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And that is not known with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is 35.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the size of the population that was enumerated in Srebrenica municipality in -- on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the difference is that 31st of March, 1991, to the fall of Srebrenica? The difference between 35.000 and 40.000 is accounted for by that time lapse, sort of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but many things happened between March 1991 and July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So it went up and down. There were people leaving Srebrenica. There were people entering Srebrenica. There were people who were born, people who died from natural causes, people who were killed, so all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the period after March of 1991 up to July 1st of 1995, for that period of some approximate four years, did you receive any objective data of a demographic nature?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. I went -- I've asked for -- I went to Tuzla. I went to many places and asked for it. I did not receive anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So with regard to the post-census pre-your study period, we have no raw information or objective information concerning births, deaths, population movement, or -- let me stop there for the moment.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. The statistical offices of -- both in Banja Luka and Sarajevo have later computerized. They had some data, some certificates of births and deaths, et cetera, and they have computerized those and made some statistics. I am not familiar with those statistics, since it did not really affect my work very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of deaths between 1991 and, once again, the beginning of July 1995, you received no hard data concerning the manner of death, and by that I mean was somebody killed as a result of conflict, did somebody die of a disease, or did they die of old age or an accident, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We have received something. There -- as I said, there has been a computerization of deaths by the statistical office in Sarajevo. So we have received some information later, after -- I don't remember the year, but it was after my -- I started this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to -- with regard to that information, can you tell us as you sit here today as to whether or not you can identify all of those deaths as being deaths which are distinct from the work that was done by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. It was badly phrased. I apologise. What I'm getting at is, can you explain for us whether or not the recognition of death -- of dead bodies by the ICMP that was done, which we're are going to talk about in a moment, that all the deaths that occurred between 1991, the time of the census, and the beginning of July exclude all of the ICMP work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that's your understanding, have you received documentation to that effect, or is that something that you obtained as a general understanding in terms of the work that you've done?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've received documentation, because the ICMP data are based on mass graves related to the fall of Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: -- and it's dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You are making some assumptions there, which I'm happy to talk with you about, but I just want to make sure, first of all, whether or not you'd received documentation that excluded whatever those particular deaths are from the ICMP work that was done, and you say you've received documentation to that effect?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I could also add that some -- we have received data sources that for a few cases indicate that some deaths may have occurred before -- or missing may have occurred before beginning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But with -- after further investigation, we conclude that most of those did not occur, say, if they are found in a Srebrenica-related mass grave. They could not have occurred before. There are a few inconsistencies remaining that are being investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- with regard to the statement that you just made, which is "... if they are found in a Srebrenica related mass grave, they could not have occurred before." I take it that there what you are doing, and understandably so, is that you're relying upon the conclusions that have been made by other individuals who are experts in other fields, for example, anthropologists or, for example, pathologists who engage in the work of DNA.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I also understand that witness statements are important on when the graves were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to now discuss the next data source that you've mentioned to us, which is the data source after 1991, which you've indicated, and I believe there were two major ones. One is the ICRC data source, and the other was the PHR data source, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The ICRC data source is a data source where you received - once again, help me; if I'm wrong, please let me know - you received questionnaires that were filled out from individuals, be they family members or friends, who related the fact that people that they knew were now missing or dead.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Almost correct, Your Honour. We did not receive the questionnaire. We received a database in electronic format containing some but not all of the information recorded on those questionnaire. I've seen empty questionnaires, that ICRC would not send us the totality of information, and neither would they send us the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They wouldn't send -- that was because some privilege issues that they felt -- some privacy issues that they felt that they had.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Privacy and neutrality issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The information that you did receive from them, that information included, as I understand it, some of the identifying characteristics that we've already talked about before.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And sometimes there was more, sometimes there was less. It all depended on the questionnaire that was filled out.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then what did you is you took the ICRC database -- or data, sorry, and you compared it with the 1991 census as well as the 1997 voter roles. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but I would say that the -- yes, it is fair, but the first thing we did was to do a consistency check and the quality check of the ICRC itself, because we received several different versions, and we had to make sure that there was no overlap and duplicates are eliminated. The same with the PHR database. They were merged into one sort of major database.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And for the first study, the 2000 study, we had not linked the whole database or missing persons to the census yet because it was complicated. That was done later. But we did link it to the voters list to look for possible survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The 2000 report was --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The 2000 report was ICRC 1997 voter list, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to return for a very quick moment to the figure you mentioned of 83 percent, which I believe dealt with the 1991 census. First of all, am I correct in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. That was the OTP 2000 list of missing persons, which was then linked to 1991 census, and we managed to link successfully with the correct certainty 83 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So there is a 17-percent -- there's a 17-percent float there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the - as you call them - identified dead, as I understand it, we have a figure now of 2.694 --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- individuals that were found, as far as you understand, in a number of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to that particular figure, as you sit here today, can you give us any further information with regard to, first, the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first I would say that there -- 103 of those were not on the list of missing persons. They are additional. That is the first. I was perhaps unclear on that earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The cause of death is not my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I know that they are found in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And that many of them were shot, but I have not looked at all of those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. I'm not quite sure I understand the witness when he says the first -- "103 of those were not on the list of missing persons. They are additional..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would be happy to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. We received from ICMP 2.694 cases of identified dead persons found in Srebrenica related graves, and those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they came from the missing list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of those, 2.591 were also found on the missing list. So there's strong evidence that there is a high degree of overlap between the ICMP lists of identified persons and the -- ICRC and also OTP lists of missing persons. But in addition, 103 people found that had not been reported to ICRC or, actually, some of them reported but we excluded them to be on the safe side because date of death and place of death or disappearance was unclear at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You added a further confusion for me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying all those -- of those 2.691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. You said of the 2.694, 2.691 were also found on the missing list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Because it was not typed in. Now, what is the difference? Is the difference between those two 103?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And you say those -- or those 103 were not on the list; you don't know where they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were excluded by us because there was some uncertainty as to the date when they went missing and the place where they went missing. So we excluded to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were never reported by their relatives as missing, perhaps because the whole family was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that number, you've told us that you cannot tell us the cause of death. Can you tell us whether or not they died during battle or not?

I cannot. That is up to the anthropologists to decide. I only know that they were found in mass graves, and many were found blindfolded or shot in ways that do not indicate armed battle; but otherwise, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, they were also found -- some were found with actual ligature on them too.
That is also the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us as you sit here today, what is the number of confirmed dead, and we'll get to that in a minute, but the number of confirmed dead that were blindfolded?
I do not know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And similarly, I take it that it would be fair to say that you do not know with regard to the issue of any ligature that they may have had near the body, correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And similarly, you could not say with regard to -- because you said people were shot, you could not tell us as you sit here today the place where they were shot or the entry of the wound that was fatal, correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'd like to do for a moment, if I could, is I'd like to go to your 2000 report, which has been identified as P404. Do you have that in front of you, sir?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Great. And in that report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have it. It would be appreciated if it could be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have -- it was going be the first page where it says "Background." We have to wait for a moment to make sure it comes up on the screen. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at the -- at the area that's called "Background," in "Background," you have a statement here, and this is something that I believe that you've been questioned about before on more than one occasion with regard to where you obtained the particular information that is set forth in the background part of your report.
That was obtained from the team working on Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.
-- as well as my own readings of books and on the fall of Srebrenica, as well as listening to testimonies or in other trials, say Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, are you -- as you sit here today, are you contending that this particular information and background is a fact which is that a number of men tried to escape by walking through the forest and many of them were killed on the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
